subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT INVOLVEMENT IN ARMX'89 ARMS BAZAAR
speechtext:
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what these people were trying to convey to us? I have the document that they left with us. I met them because I believe that they are representing a very important organization. Here is what they told us:
As former military people who have put our lives on the line for democracy, the undersigned are concerned that Canada's agenda for NATO's May 29-30 meeting has not yet been discussed in Parliament. The subject is far too critical to be decided behind closed doors.
I agree with them. That is why I told them that I would indeed raise the matter today. They continued:
NATO's choice about "modernization" of short-range nuclear
weapons will reveal whether it aims at diminishing the risk of war, or at
prolonging the burdens and risks of the arms race.
May 19, 1989

The challenge is to propose to the Warsaw Pact mutual arms reductions in all aspects of the military confrontation. This is what Norway, West Germany, and other European allies want.
At the same time, powerful forces want NATO to upgrade its Lance missiles and nuclear artillery, especially to encourage the U.S. Congress to fund more new nuclear weapons. These people want the arms race to continue.
The May 29-30 NATO decision can be a major step toward international co-operation and the elimination of war or it can be a dispiriting rebuff to Mr. Gorbachev's constructive acts and proposals.
Forty years ago, it was Canada that insisted (in Article 2 of the Tleaty) that NATO be more than a military alliance. It is Canada's opportunity now to carry this farther, by insisting that NATO initiate NATO/Warsaw Pact co-operation in resolving world environmental and economic problems. Negative and obsolete militarism must not be allowed to win the day.

That was the message conveyed to us this week by the Veterans' Association Against Nuclear Arms. We of the Liberal Party received them and listened to them attentively. Furthermore, I wanted to transmit their viewpoint to the House as soon as possible. I think it is unacceptable and most regrettable that neither the Minister or the Associate Minister nor any Member of the Conservative government cared to meet with them or listened to their viewpoint. It is obvious that the NATO meeting at the end of May will be an important and historic event.
The Minister said a few moments ago that she wants to stand by her NATO friends. What friends? As we well know, there is presently quite a split among NATO members. Canada played a very important role in the setting up of NATO and rightly insisted that Section 2 of the NATO Charter should not address exclusively the military character of the organization, but also its economic and political responsibilities. We think that NATO is a very important tool. Unlike the New Democratic Party, we do not want Canada to withdraw from NATO. We believe that we should belong to the Alliance.
The Official Opposition, the Liberal Party, wants Canada to remain in NATO, but we want NATO to play not only a military role, but a political and economic role as well, as was initially intended. We think that the recent initiatives by Secretary General Gorbachev offer us an ideal opportunity to bring about a rapprochement between the members of NATO and the members of the Warsaw Pact.
At a time when there is much talk about peace, at a time when organizations such as the one I have just mentioned want more harmonious relations between the peoples of the earth, the Minister promotes an arms
Supply
trade show as if it were a great and wonderful thing. I say she is out of touch with present-day reality.
People are craving for peace, they are completely overwhelmed by all those nuclear weapons threatening their safety, 24 hours a day. The people of the world, not the governments, do not want to hear speeches like the one the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mrs. Collins) just gave us praise of arms sales and new defence technologies. That is not what we want. We want peace! We want people to realize what is going on in the world! We just have to put an end to this crazy arms race, to this quest for new weapons. We don't want that, we don't even want to hear about it!
We regret that this government which is supposed to be going through a very serious budget crisis- Since each and every minister, and especially the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), have been telling us all week long that Canada is facing an important deficit which has top priority, and that we have to cut government expenditures, I wonder why the Government did not simply decide to cut funds to this arms bazaar. That would have set a good example and would have been a good way to cut down on expenses. Instead, we are setting display booths and sending representatives who will spend the whole week giving out pamphlets and overseeing the arms exhibition, at a time when we could be dealing with more important things!
Finally, I just want to add that it is obvious the arms produced in Canada are, directly or indirectly, finding their way to developing countries, to Third World countries.

The highly profitable trade in high-tech weaponry from the north to the south, always justified on ideological grounds whether real or contrived, has transformed dozens and dozens of regimes around the world into heavily equipped arsenals. We know for sure that the Russians are expending a lot of effort to sell some of their weapons in the Third World. We think that it is unacceptable. As conventional disarmament takes hold in Europe there is the dangerous risk that arms will be released to Third World markets at bargain basement prices, involving thousands of lethal weapons ranging from battle tanks to heavy artillery. All the while in developing country after developing country alert to the profitable circumstances of weapons manufacturers in the western world, we find that industrialized output is being geared to military hardware.

speechtext:
I hope the right hon. gentleman is watching.
Canada produces military equipment in order to meet our defence needs and our obligations under NATO and NORAD. To purchase these goods from other countries, which is what the Opposition seems to be suggesting, would be financially onerous and would hamper our ability to equip Canada's forces. It would also deny
May 19, 1989

Canadian industry the technological and industrial benefits that are associated with defence production, and deny Canadian workers the jobs that would be created.
Defence acquisition takes place in a highly controlled environment to ensure the best possible value for the operational requirement of the Armed Forces and the best possible return on investment for the taxpayers. In recent years, all major DND acquisitions have included an industrial benefits component that includes technology transfer, new investment, job creation all across Canada, from Newfoundland to British Columbia. The Defence White Paper clearly sets out the development of a defence industrial base as one of the foundations of an effective defence.
We now have some 540 companies involved in the industry and close to 40,000 Canadians employed in these companies manufacturing defence and civilian products. Many of these industries that have evolved in Canada have developed technologies that are relevant to civil applications; particularly electronics and avionics. Relatively few defence products manufactured in this country can be classified as offensive military equipment.
The increasing complexity and high cost of modem military systems are such that it is not possible for Canada to undertake most major development projects on its own. Thus the nature of Canada's industry has become one of supplying subsystems and components, co-operating with other allies in the development of co-operative programs other than supplying weapon systems as such. Over the years, Canadian companies have developed an expertise that is recognized the world over. They are sought out by our treaty partners for systems developed by them. I do not need to tell the House that the lion's share of our trade in defence goods takes places with our NATO allies and other friendly nations. Approximately 97 per cent of our exports of military goods went to OECD countries in 1988.
These countries have, like Canada, a legitimate defence requirement as our partners in a defence alliance and to exercise their right to legitimate self defence. Our exports to these countries not only reduces the cost burden on Canadian taxpayers and the Government by extending production lines and reducing costs, but they
Supply
satisfy our defence objectives by contributing to standardization and inter-operability. It also ensures that NATO defence forces have equipment that we know to be reliable and state-of-the-art. It follows that if we produce this equipment, and we want to keep costs down and the industry viable, we will also want to encourage other countries to purchase the equipment.
Canadian exhibitors at ARMX have every right to demonstrate their capability to potential customers. We encourage them to do so, and support them in their marketing activity. However, we also control them and to whom they sell. I will return to this a little later.
A close examination of Canada's defence industry will reveal that we produce very little bellicose equipment. Those defence goods that we do produce have earned us an enviable reputation around the world for civil applications. One need only cite simulator technology, short take-off and landing aircraft, navigation systems and communication technology.
Press reports and the rhetoric surrounding the show which I mentioned earlier, have alleged that Canadian firms sell vomit gas. That was one of the claims that was being made; something else to abuse the rights of civilians. The Hon. Member from Spadina (Mr. Heap) is probably one of the greatest abusers of misinformation. He likes to talk about things of which he knows very little, and does not always have the facts at his fingertips. I am sure we will hear from him later today. But nothing is further from the truth. A responsible student of the issue will know that Canada does not produce these gases or any other crowd control gases. We have stringent controls on the export of all military and paramilitary goods.
All Members of the House should be familiar with Canada's export control policies which were announced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in 1986. These controls are amongst the most stringent in the world, and they work. In his meeting with the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade just last week, the Secretary of State for External Affairs invited that committee to look into our arms export policy. Perhaps a review by the committee could also review some of the rhetoric that surrounds this issue and help people understand that Canada not only has a

May 19, 1989
Supply
responsible policy in this complex area, but also helps interested Canadians recognize that our policy works.
I repeat that invitation here today on behalf of my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I would like to see the committee get involved in this.
In the few minutes left to me, Mr. Speaker, I want to talk about our export control policies as they apply to military goods, and as they reflect the views and objectives of the Canadian people.
Canadians recognize our need to respect our defence obligations. They recognize our desire for international order and stability and they take a strong stand against human rights abuse. Specifically the policy is biased to deny export of all military goods and technology to, first, countries that pose a threat to Canada and its allies; second, countries involved in or under imminent threat of hostilities; third, countries under United Nations security council sanctions; and fourth, countries whose governments have a persistent record of violations of the human rights of their citizens, unless it can be demonstrated that there is no reasonable risk that the goods might be used against the civilian population.
Those are the cold facts. But in reality our scrutiny does not stop there. We review every overseas export transaction for military goods. As part of that review, we assess the human rights record of the country of destination. We verify security concerns, and examine the regional stability implications of these transactions. In a large number of cases, the export permit must be reviewed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs himself.
Once a permit is issued, trained officials seek assurances that goods are destined to bona fide clients and verify the veracity of these transactions. This scrutiny of export transactions is not restricted to weapons or arms, but covers all goods that could reasonably contribute to a military capability. This could include goods that are specifically designed or adapted to military purposes such as military vehicles or goods made to mill specs and components thereto. I heard my hon. friend talking about helicopters earlier on. These goods are defined in the export control list and were developed with our partners in COCOM.
COCOM is the co-ordinating committee on multilateral strategic export controls. Those are our NATO allies plus the country of Japan.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that my time is drawing to a close. I would like to say this; that the foregoing should assure the Hon. Members and the Canadian public that Canada is not, and will not, become the source of arms for nations that would abuse human rights. ARMX is a show that highlights simulation and training equipment. Both are areas where Canada possesses particular expertise; high-tech, developed and produced in Canada, and why not, and why should we not use them?
Exhibitors are targeting the requirements of Canada's Armed Forces. Although visitors from other nations are invited to view Canadian capabilities, Canadian industry is well aware of the constraints placed on it by Canada's export control policies.
We are confident that this particular show is a very important show for Canada, for Canadians, for our Aimed Forces, for industry, for those workers who work there, and we have no objections to this being carried on by the private sector.

I listened carefully to the Hon. Minister. I was particularly interested in his latter remarks about the controls on exports. I did not hear him say that we place an end-use requirement which the United States does to require the buying country to testify in a legally binding manner as to what will be the end use.
In other words, when we sell goods to the United States, for example, helicopters or helicopter parts, we do not know whether they will wind up sold or given by the United States to the Contras in Nicaragua, or to the Salvadoran army in El Salvador to strafe and bomb civilians.
The same applies when we sell aeroplane engines to Israel or Brazil, and later hear that they have been sold to Governments such as the Governments of Honduras, El Salvador, or to the Contras. It appears quite legal for those countries to do this because we have not required any statement from them about end use.
When the Minister talked about the restriction on exports to certain countries in certain categories, and spoke about countries with a persistent record of violence against their citizens, unless it can be shown that there is no danger of the goods being used that way, he did not mention that the Government has refused to identify which countries are currently under that restriction. Therefore, it is impossible for us to evaluate how

subjective or accurate the Government's identification may be. Does it include El Salvador in such a list? We do not know.
Finally, the Minister did not explain why the Government altered its practice with respect to access to information. When there have been inquiries about exports to certain countries, the information that is returned consists of stating that "deleted" sent "deleted" to "deleted". In other words, they do not want any further embarrassment such as that encountered by the previous Government about the tank parts to Chile.
Perhaps the Minister would be willing to explain why the Government is so secretive about this policy of which it is so proud, and why it neglects to secure the end use of its products in the same way as does our ally the United States?

The Government spends a considerable amount of time consulting with NGO groups, the non-government organizations that work around the world in many beneficial ways and are on the ground in most of these countries and know what is going on. They provide a tremendous amount of information to the Government. They let us know about the human rights developments

in countries. We are very appreciative of that type of support.
The House will remember that one of the last acts of the House last fall was to approve the establishment of an International Institute of Human Rights and Democratic Development. We do not turn our backs on those principles when it comes to military exports. If my friend thought about it and fully examined what we do, I am sure he would agree that we are extremely strict in this country about exports.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT INVOLVEMENT IN ARMX'89 ARMS BAZAAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the advantages of being in the Liberal Party is that it is the very embodiment of light and reason. One of the entertaining things we have watched in this House today is the difficulty that is faced by the Government on the one hand because it has caught itself in a very embarrassing situation with the ARMX bazaar next week, and the New Democratic Party tiying its best to abandon its unusual policies.
We have seen much back-pedalling on both sides, and many attempts to shuffle and cover over the facts. I am delighted the Minister of State for Privatization (Mr. McDermid) is here. I enjoyed his speech today, and I will undoubtedly refer to some of his remarks again.
I want to start with my friends on the left because it is their motion we are discussing today. It has to be one of the most back-pedalling motions I have seen in a long time. It will not say what is the position of the Party. We are getting different stories.
This morning the person who would like to be leader of that Party, the Hon. Member for Regina-Qu'Appelle (Mr. de Jong), made his foray into the leadership race. He spoke very eloquently but, of course, was not really spouting the same line that the Hon. Member for Esquimau Juan de Fuca (Mr. Barrett) was espousing with his comments to the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mrs. Collins). Now we are hearing a different view for the benefit of Edmonton East. They are all over the place.
When we hear from the Hon. Member for Trinity- Spadina (Mr. Heap) later, I expect he will give a different version as well. In other words, there is a complete lack of coherent policy.
I am sure that is the reason for this vaguely worded resolution we are discussing today. I want to read part of it:

That this House condemn the government's involvement in the
arms bazaar, ARMX'89, and calls upon the government:
(1) to cease all involvement in the expansion of the international market for military and policing equipment; and
(2) to take action to ensure that countries which violate human rights are prohibited from directly or indirectly arranging purchases of military and policing equipment in Canada.-Mr. de Jong.

What does all that mean? What are we supposed to take from this? Are they in favour of ARMX, or are they against ARMX?
They say that they are opposed to the Government's involvement in it, but they do not say anything about ARMX itself. They are not sure. Some of them will be against it and some of them will not.
The Hon. Member for Regina-Qu'Appelle certainly did not condemn the exhibition this morning. He was speaking in wonderful sentences about how it was a shame that it was happening, but he did not say he wanted it stopped. He did not urge the Government to
May 19, 1989

discontinue it. He urged the Government to stop supporting it, and that is as far as he would go. We keep getting different stories.
I had a New Democratic Party opponent whose views I am sure Hon. Members have heard. Major General Johnson was their principal defence critic throughout the last election campaign. We had a lot of discussions in Kingston about defence matters, with good reason. Kingston has a large Canadian forces base, which fortunately has not been closed down by recent government cut-backs and is also the home of the Royal Military College, one of Canada's finest educational institutions. I am honoured to represent those two bodies in this House.
It is made much easier to represent it because of the party position we have in these matters, which I will turn to in a moment.
It is important that we look at the views the New Democratic Party has attempted to express.
The Hon. Member for Regina Qu'Appelle gave his very long-winded exposition this morning. He spoke about the evils of the arms race, which everyone concedes, and spoke about the virtues of peace, which everyone recognizes. He really did not say very much about the resolution or about the New Democratic Party policy. I think the reason is apparent. I hope that there will be some clarification of what their policy may or may not be during some of the speeches later.
The Government's position in this matter is equally ambiguous. I want to deal with some of the difficulties in terms of what has been said here this afternoon and what is happening with respect to this exhibition. What is this exhibition or bazaar? As the Associate Minister of National Defence said earlier, it is a bazaar for training and simulation technology and for defence technology for the 21st century. That is what is advertised on the brochure.
It appears that this exhibition was formerly sponsored by the Government. Perhaps the Minister of State for Privatization can tell us why this was changed, because he is privatizing everything by selling the assets of the Canadian people back to them.
The Government has decided not to run ARMX as a government function any longer and to let the private sector run it. I can understand the Government's reluc-

tance. The questions being asked, particularly by New Democratic Party Members in the House today, clearly are causing the Government some embarrassment. It decided that the best course of action was to put it in private hands in order to deflect the criticism to others, so it will not have to answer for any of the mistakes that might be made. That is the kind of attitude that typifies the Progressive Conservative Party. Instead of standing up and admitting mistakes or that things are not the way they ought to be, they say it is not their responsibility and try to shirk that responsibility. That has been happening in the House for some weeks.
My constituents have written many letters to many government Departments in an attempt to find out what is happening at ARMX. In many cases the replies were four to six weeks in coming. In many cases there were no replies at all. Ultimately they approached me to take up the matter with government Departments.
They brought me a petition containing over 200 names. Unfortunately, I will be unable to table it in the House because it is not in the proper form, but they indicated in it their opposition to this exhibition and their dissatisfaction with the answers they were receiving on the matter.
Among other things, they urged me to take steps and write to the various government Departments to find out what, in fact, was happening.
I have a letter I received from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. McKnight), which basically reaffirms the position taken in the House today by the Associate Minister of National Defence. Let me read it to the House to illume the House on this matter. The Minister writes:
The purpose of this letter is to respond to your inquiry of March 6, 1989 on the subject of ARMX '89.
I should say that this letter is dated April 27, to give an idea of the length of time it takes to get information together on ARMX. There is clearly a problem. The letter goes on:
At the outset, it is important to realize that ARMX '89 is a private sector undertaking sponsored by Baxter Publications. The exhibit itself focuses on technology, related to training simulator and procedures for military applications. As such, it features Canadian and international industry demonstrating training technology equipment and simulators devices. The Department of National Defence's interest in ARMX '89 is exclusively related to obtaining as much information as possible on this training technology in order that we may better train our personnel in a more cost effective manner. DND's participation is confined to stating future training

May 19, 1989

requirements in the form of presentations at a seminar program and a booth display.

She took the bull by the horns and wrote directly to Baxter Publications, at least I presume it was them. It was certainly the name and address given me by the Minister of National Defence. Thank you for your letter of February 16,1989, and your interest in ARMX.
ARMX as you may know is Canada's Defence Equipment Exhibition featuring simulation and training technology. It is only open to military, government, police and defence industry representatives. is privileged information. Should you be eligible to apply as a visitor, please let me know and I will send you the application form.

Your company can be right in the centre of intense buying action.
With no general public in attendance, each delegate is a bona fide
buyer, prospect or user. The time you spend with them will be the
most effective and productive of the year.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT INVOLVEMENT IN ARMX'89 ARMS BAZAAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Mr. Milliken) was not here at the beginning or did not take the time carefully to read our motion. I think it is quite clear and I will read it for his benefit and for anybody else who would like to know what it is.
Our motion is:
That this House condemn the government's involvement in the
arms bazaar, ARMX '89, and calls upon the government:
(1)	to cease all involvement in the expansion of the international market for military and policing equipment; and
(2)	to take action to ensure that countries which violate human rights are prohibited from directly or indirectly arranging purchases of military and policing equipment in Canada.
That presents difficulty only to those who want to cast the NDP in the position of total and absolute pacifism and then express mock surprise when they find that while we have pacifists in the Party, the Party by policy is not pacifist but, in fact, is a Party that undertakes to promote peace and to keep militarization to the minimum that is needed for defence, and not to use militarization as a means of enrichment. That is perhaps what the Hon. Member has not been able to learn but it is clear enough from the way we worded our motion.
I want to give a little description of this armaments exhibition, explain what I think is wrong with this rationale, what I think would be a better rationale for an approach and an alternative.
In its description I think it could be reasonably said that the representation of the evil empire will be in Ottawa next week. President Reagan once said that the Soviet Union is the evil empire. He changed his mind. The Leader of Iran has said the United States is the evil empire, or the satanic empire, but some of his supporters
Supply
are not clear about that. I am not suggesting that any government is an evil empire. I am suggesting that the arms race itself and the very great powers that support it, those that President Eisenhower on his retirement called the military industrial complex, collectively constitute an evil empire.
Governments are currently promoting the spending of $1.2 trillion on armaments, while nearly half the world's people go hungry. They could be well fed with much left over if even part of that $1.2 trillion were diverted from arms to more constructive uses.
The Government, as was pointed out, has been curiously defensive. It wants to suggest that this has nothing to do with selling arms. I give the Member for Kingston and The Islands (Mr. Milliken) full credit for having clearly explained from the Government's own document that, in fact, as he quoted "Your company can be right in on the centre of intense buying action", and so on and so forth.
There is also the letter in the program from the Chief of Defence Staff, General P. D. Manson, "As in past years the ARMX exhibition will have a special Canadian Forces focus following on from the Government of Canada's 1987 White Paper on Defence, Challenge and Commitment. Canadian Forces have entered a period of revitalization, restructuring and re-equipment. These advances will generate unique training systems and equipment requirements which will be defined in the Canadian Forces exhibits and seminars during ARMX '89".
In other words, it is not as the Minister would have us believe, just training. It is training and equipment. Of course, modem equipment requires modem training. There is no mystery about that.
I listed earlier for the Minister's information a few of the exhibitors advertised in the program which are involved in anything but peaceful activities. They are producing weapons that kill people. I did not have time to continue but I will give just a few more.
General Dynamics from the United States produces the Stinger, a shoulder launched fire and forget missile. That company will be there, according to the Government statement at least.

May 19, 1989
Supply
Invar Manufacturing will display a designed armoured launching turret for tow missile systems. Well, a launching turret does not sound like a training or a simulation system, it sounds like something that will launch, something that will kill people, or if you aim right will kill people.
Junghans Feinwerktechnik from West Germany, are producers of mechanical and electronic fuses for automatic cannon, mortar and artillery ammunition, fuses for rockets, missiles, AT weapons, mines, and so on. There are plenty more exhibitors that produce weaponry. The Government's attempt to suggest that that is not true certainly helps to encourage the suspicions of the public who wonder what is going on.
In fact, what we have here is an arrangement for sale, granted they will not take tanks home their knapsacks, but both the equipment and the training systems can become part of regimes which are suppressing their civilian populations. The Government will be teaching methods of killing and suppression and control. Some of those methods have already been used in countries like Chile.
The Government claims that it has a good system of follow-up to make sure that our equipment does not go astray to any such country, but in fact, Project Ploughshares, a national research organization-the Minister will complain, of course, that it is funded by the church or churches.
The Minister of State for Privatization (Mr. McDer-mid) will complain that the churches have an interest, and I do not know whether he thinks they make money out of this or not, but in fact, Project Ploughshares has for many years been a well-respected peace organization. They estimate that $150 million to $200 million worth of Canadian arms components find their way into the Third World annually through other countries. This was printed in The Ottawa Citizen in January. Canadian arms exported to the United States have ended up in Iran, South Korea, Honduras and Paraguay, all human rights violators, according to Amnesty International.
The Government's follow-up system does not work very well and it is very unwise of the Government to be so secretive about its prohibition list because, clearly, the
Government cannot do its job properly without the help of Canadian citizens who support the prohibition that the Government claims it has enacted.
This arms bazaar is being conducted in keeping and with the implicit support, of course, of the Free Trade Agreement which exempted only two kinds of subsidies to be used by the Canadian Government. One is a subsidy on energy and the other is a subsidy on armaments. Section 2003 of the Free Trade Agreement clearly encourages and gives the green light to the Government to use arms production as the only job opportunity for Canadians in very depressed areas of Canada. This, of course, plus the $250 million worth of annual grants to arms producers, is the main basis for holding ARMX. Granted, now they are able to funnel the profits to Baxter Publishing, but in fact, it would not be happening without Government encouragement, without this brochure in which the Government participates, without the military being there from all three services. ARMX would not be happening without the Government's participation, and that is why our motion condemns the Government for promoting that sort of thing.
I will not go into the list of companies who receive DIP grants and are exhibiting here. Some of them have already been mentioned. I would rather go on to a further point and that is the list of countries for whom arms export permits are given under the Export Control Act. They include India, just last year nearly $83 million worth; South Korea, just last year nearly $162 million worth; Pakistan, $1 million; Peru, $3 million; Turkey, $17 million; Zaire, $7.5 million. Our country has been exporting to these governments, although they all have very serious records of human rights violations. Yet-

It is very difficult to find out. The Minister hollers, what were the products. It is very difficult to find out when we send for the information and we get the reply, after paying the fee, that "deleted sent deleted to deleted". The Government does not want us to know what they are sending to those countries.
May 19, 1989

I will give just a few instances of some of these countries from Amnesty International. We mentioned Chile already, but for example, in El Salvador, there were arrests of suspected government opponents, some of whom were supposedly tortured, subjected to severe psychological pressure or extra-judicially executed, some of whom disappeared while in custody. What we are told publicly is that anyone who is accredited to Ottawa, any diplomat accredited to Ottawa is invited to attend. In other words, to that extent, all these countries that are human rights violators are invited to attend. While of course they cannot carry away a tank in their knapsack, as Colonel North said, in fact they can make contacts and place orders. Guatemala has the same sort of record.
Apparently Israel has a Canadian subsidiary that is exhibiting here. In December, at least 23 Palestinian demonstrators in the West Bank and Gaza were shot and killed-this is a report of the previous year-by soldiers during widespread violent protests against the Israeli occupation. There were also severe and indiscriminate beatings of demonstrators and hundreds were summarily tried and imprisoned. There was an increase in reports of ill-treatment and torture of detainees by members of the Israeli defence force and the general security service. Yet Israel is invited to exhibit here and Israel is free to attend and make arrangements for buying.
In fact, it appears that the primary object of the arms bazaar is not to equip the Canadian Army. We would not need 13,000 visitors which the Government says it is expecting to equip the Canadian Army. In fact, I think the clear object of this is simply to make higher profits for arms producing companies, including Canadian ones, and to make those profits without regard to what happens with the weapons that are sold. This is what I object to and what our Party objects to and what is clearly opposed in the statement that we produced last spring called "Canada's Stake in Common Security". We object to having the manufacture of armaments done primarily or solely for profit or perhaps solely for profit with the only condition that it stays within the general guidelines of NATO. I say general because obviously our weaponry gets to countries who are not in NATO but perhaps through NATO partners. Otherwise, it is a matter of profit.
Supply
Indirectly, also, technological growth in turn increases the power to make profit, but the key question is profit. I would like to point out that more and more economists are pointing out the flaws in the theory that building up armaments builds up the general economy and the industrial strength of our country. It has been pointed out that in recent studies done under the United Nations and in the United States, countries such as Japan and Germany with the least investment in weaponry, that is in production of war goods, have a better industrial performance, a more efficient industrial performance, than the United States does. For Canada, of course, with our DPSA agreement with the United States, any jobs that we gained by selling to the United States are balanced by jobs that go to the United States when we buy from them. We are only supposed to sell as much as we buy. Actually we sell less than we buy. So the sale arrangement is not one that increases the jobs in Canada. We simply at best exchange jobs with the United States.
There is also, Mr. Speaker, what has been found by experience; that the technological spin-offs from military development are not very important, not very useful. In fact, that is one of the reasons why Japan and Germany have been able to progress faster than the United States and Canada in their economies.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are indicating to me that my time is running out. I want to finish by pointing out that it is possible to plan for a transition from war production that is not needed to peace production, production in the broadest sense. That does not appear to have occurred to the Government in connection with its closure or announcement that it will close certain bases. It does not appear to have made provision for alternative economy or alternative employment. It can be done. It was done in the United States and Canada after World War II, quite successfully. If you are not interested in making highest profits, that is what we should be doing. Instead of promoting, as this armaments exhibition does, just mindless increase in the sales of weaponry, we should be choosing after public debate what kind of weapons we need to defend our country and the ones that can be least used to threaten others with attack.

May 19, 1989

Then we should be considering what is necessary to produce those and direct the rest of our resources to meeting the needs of the one-sixth of the people in our country who are under the poverty line and the needs of the aboriginal peoples of our country. We would find we have some left over to meet the needs of the countries that were recently colonies of Europe that have been pillaged and need to be allowed to stand on their feet.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT INVOLVEMENT IN ARMX'89 ARMS BAZAAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think one of the benefits of this debate has been the furthering of my knowledge of what ARMX is all about. I appreciate the comments of my colleague here and also the colleagues across the floor and on the NDP side of the House. We have heard quite a distinct divergence of views this afternoon. It has certainly lifted some of the aura of indecision and confusion that seems to lie around the ARMX bazaar that is happening shortly in Ottawa. If I could move off ARMX for a moment, I would like to briefly comment on where we stand as a nation today in world military spending. We all know we spend more than 25 times what we spend on foreign aid to the developing nations of the world, and that weapons imports now amount to 25 per cent of the total debt burden of the developing world. I think this is something that concerns us all.
I believe it is incumbent upon us all to ensure that Canada has a multilateral approach to peace in the world, and working with other nations and other peoples is surely the best way to ensure peace and prosperity for all. The question that we all should be asking ourselves is how Canada can best contribute most effectively in the search for global peace. One of the key problem areas is the existence of nuclear weapons. We should all be working toward their reduction and the means to ensure that the East-West conflict will not occur.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT INVOLVEMENT IN ARMX'89 ARMS BAZAAR

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT INVOLVEMENT IN ARMX'89 ARMS BAZAAR
speechtext:
There is no question that Canada should not get into the game of mass producing military weapons for export abroad. One of the things that the Free Trade Agreement does is it threatens the capacity of Canadians to pursue an independent foreign policy. The question I would like to ask my colleague is this. Looking at the NDP policy with regards to the arms race and peace in the world, I am wondering if he as an NDP still rejects Canada's view that we should be neutralist in our commitment to NATO. Also would he not agree that we
as Canadians should continue our commitment to our NATO friends abroad?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT INVOLVEMENT IN ARMX'89 ARMS BAZAAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in fact as the statement that we adopted a year ago last month lays out, we believe that NATO has outlived its usefulness for peace and that it is now one of the embodiments of a sort of unthinking momentum toward the arms race. Our policy is that in the first year of government, we would withdraw our troops from Europe. We would continue with the political side of NATO until perhaps a second term. The decisions could be made as we continue along, but what was clear and unambiguous in that statement is that we would withdraw our troops at the beginning of an NDP Government.
I think that is an important signal. When we began debating this in public, that is to say when certain journalists affected great surprise at discovering an NDP policy which had existed since 1969, what we found was it generated a great deal of discussion, not only on the left in Canada, but amongst people who are not considered to be on the left, and we find there is a great deal of debate within the United States and Europe about the usefulness of NATO. There are some alliances that do not last forever, and it is fairly clear that NATO will not. Therefore what we propose is that Canada should first of all restrict itself in such things as having nuclear ships visit our ports, testing potentially nuclear missiles and quartering troops in central Europe. Those are now quite unnecessary for the defence of Europe and quite ineffective for the defence of Canada, but they are provocations which continue to justify other countries in building up or maintaining their armaments. At the present time there is the chance of reducing armaments, and this is the kind of action that Canada should be taking.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT INVOLVEMENT IN ARMX'89 ARMS BAZAAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter before us today deals with a bazaar, and the debate attached to it seemingly becomes more bizarre as the afternoon progresses. I would suspect that the next time a CF-18 patrols the skies of Canada for defence purposes that unless we hold a national referendum to disclose publicly the purpose of that aircraft in the air, the aircraft will not be permitted to take off.
Today is an opposition day. The subject the Opposition has chosen to place before us certainly leaves me, as it apparently has left many Members, not the least of whom are those who authored this motion, with a certain lack of interest. When given that opportunity, as the Opposition has today, and when looking at the essence of
Supply
the motion, one must certainly conclude what a wasted day it is.
We have a national debt problem that consumes 35 cents out of every dollar of revenue received by the Government of Canada. This is an ideal opportunity for the Opposition to place before the House some solutions. What do we hear? Nothing. This is an ideal opportunity for members of the NDP to put before the House some of their plans in relation to women's rights or equity in the workplace. What do we hear? Nothing.
Members of the NDP said that our plan for day care did not go far enough and that it was not comprehensive enough. This is an ideal opportunity for them to provide us with solutions. What do we hear? Nothing. Members of the NDP have stated in the past that perhaps the development of a long-term agricultural policy would be necessary. This is an ideal opportunity to present something to this House. There is no rain, just a lot of hot air. The problem is that members of the NDP have been in opposition so long that there is no air or thought of positiveness or constructive development in their minds.
I am pleased to discuss the issue of ARMX as has been done so eloquently by my fellow Members. ARMX has received much media attention in the past week. I have been hearing that ARMX is a Department of National Defence sponsored event which promotes the use of military violence. There is simply nothing that could be further from the truth. ARMX is not in the least linked to violence. In fact, ARMX does quite the contrary. It is a privately run trade show. I have been associated with many privately run trade shows, and there is nothing unique about this one. It is designed to bring industry and government together in the field of training and simulation technology.
All the nonsense we have heard points to a great need for the record to be set straight. I will endeavour to do that very thing. I would like to provide the House with another history in order that how and why ARMX was created might sink in and to explain the importance of ARMX to Canadian industry.
ARMX or the Armed Forces Training Technology Exhibition which is exactly what it is, is a biannual exhibition of training and simulation technology for the Armed Forces. It began in 1983 and it has been held every two years since. I would like to draw to the attention of my colleagues that, as few as seven years ago, no trade show for the military even existed in Canada. One may or may not like spending money on the military. One may choose to object to equipping the

May 19, 1989
Supply
forces we need to help to defend democracy. One may not deny that if we are to have forces at all for peacekeeping as well as to help ensure deterrence, we will need arms. If we need arms, why should we always have to buy them abroad?
The main force behind the first ARMX was the Canadian Land Forces increasing interest in the cost effectiveness of simulators for training. Simulators require no fuel, no ammunition, and less maintenance than tanks, artillery, and other equipment.
Lieutenant-Colonel Stuart Northrup was given the formidable task of organizing the first ARMX. In his view, and I ask Members to bear in mind that he had great experience, a trade show format was the most effective way of putting the available technologies in front of the right people. Having decided on the venue, he now had to convince officials of the Department of National Defence to support and fund the project. It was the Commander of Mobile Command who first agreed to host this ground breaking event.
The army training technology exhibition began in 1983 when it held its first exhibition in St. Hubert, Quebec. Its focus was then, and remains today, on training and training simulation technology. Although ARMX initially offered simulator technology for the Army only, some 65 exhibitors from eight countries were present. They helped draw more than 3,000 military and civilian visitors.
The exhibition was created for no other reason than to permit members of the Canadian Forces to make contact with industry and discuss what training technology was forthcoming, and obviously to afford the industry the benefit of the user's view of current requirements. It also gave industry an opportunity to meet government officials at various levels and to inform them of the newest technologies available.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you have deplored as I have the lack of contact between industry and government, the other two solitudes. I am sure that you will
readily agree that anything that helps bridge the gap between them is positive.
In turn, ARMX has provided government with an opportunity to compare all the newest technologies from all the companies in one place. For both industry and government it provided insight into which way the other was moving. Ideas could be exchanged formally, comparisons could be made not only among the companies, but also their countries. Naturally, this led to savings on both sides. As we all know, we can do with some serious savings in this country.
Two years later ARMX '85 was held at CFB Ottawa in the spring of 1985. Because of its success two years earlier, it expanded to include all three branches of the Canadian Forces, Army, Air Force, and Navy. ARMX had by now grown to include 251 exhibitors from 20 countries, who saw it as an opportunity for foreign country corporations to sell to Canada and for Canadian companies to promote export capabilities and their products to the Canadian Government.
When I mention exports, it must be clear to all who sit in the House that we have one of the most stringent policies in the world to restrict the flow of armaments, not only to countries involved or that could soon be involved in hostilities, but to states with objectionable records in the field of human rights. In a news release from the Department of External Affairs dated September 10, 1986 it states:
The Minister stressed that Canada will not allow the export of military equipment to countries whose governments have a persistent record of serious violations of the human rights of their citizens, unless it can be demonstrated that there is no reasonable risk that the goods might be used against the civilian population: "The new policy with respect to countries with serious human rights problems places the onus of proving 'no reasonable risk' squarely on the exporter".
That has to be underscored because there are those in this country who would have the public believe that we export indiscriminately, or that exporting helmets somehow amounts to arms sales. Unfortunately, some members of the Opposition have been known not to set the record straight when they have had the opportunity to do so.
Obviously, the other countries participating in ARMX '85 saw the benefit of participating in this type of trade show. They saw it as a way of gaining valuable information on Canadian security needs and in making contacts not only with Canadian industry but Canadian government officials.
May 19, 1989

That was about the time when the Department of National Defence decided that while the need for ARMX was valid, there were good reasons why the Department of National Defence should privatize it. I would like to repeat some of those reasons here today.
First, as the exhibition grew in size and scope, it required more and more DND staff. This did not seem to make the best use of the Department's already scarce resources. It did seem, however, to put to extremely good use the industries' resources. Second, since it had come to an industry led forum, it seemed only proper that industry should become the primary organizer.
Finally, it was apparent by now that if we were to continue to sponsor ARMX, this could be misinterpreted by the public. Apparently, that is so. Certainly, in recent years we have seen how the so-called peace groups, although tiny, have managed to grab the attention of the public simply by making a lot of noise and by clouding the fact that the largest of the genuine peace groups in this country is the Canadian Forces. Ask the United Nations. Ask the Nobel Peace Prize Committee.
The most recent example of this which comes to mind is the very odd and, I must say, perhaps somewhat shameful decision of the Ottawa City Council to deny city owned sites for future ARMXs. Is it not a shame to think that we may be denied this great opportunity to deal informally with industry all because ARMX is misunderstood?
Mind you, if the City of Ottawa feels that ARMX should not be held there, I am sure that my riding could offer an equally, if not better, place for ARMX '91. Perhaps Canadian Forces Base Moose Jaw might be interested. Perhaps the Government should consider moving all military related functions out of Ottawa. Why not? It is apparently asking for that to happen.
At that point in 1985, an agreement was concluded between the Minister of National Defence and Defence Publications Limited, one of a group of companies directed by Baxter Publications in Toronto. This company, one of three that bid for the right to take over the ARMX name and run the exhibition, is well known to us through the publishing of the Defence Quarterly magazine. We should all be made aware of the significant
Supply
contribution Baxter Publications makes through its Canadian Defence Quarterly magazine.
There are few people with any knowledge of defence who do not read it regularly. I strongly encourage all Members opposite to do so as well. They may not enjoy all the articles, but they will learn a thing or two, thanks to the review's excellent coverage of Canadian defence issues.
In June, 1986, the agreement transferred to Defence Publications Limited the right to use the ARMX name and goodwill and to organize and run an exhibition which was to have as its theme training and training simulation.
Given the importance of this agreement and the recent attention ARMX has received in the media, I want to take this opportunity to read some of the more significant clauses:
It is agreed by both parties that the Minister of National Defence shall in no way be responsible for the promotion, operation or managing of ARMX.
It is agreed by both parties that the Minister of National Defence shall have no obligation to provide ARMX with any financial, logistic or personnel support, nor shall the Minister be obligated to provide any physical facilities and/or equipment for the operation of ARMX.
Defence Publications limited agrees to assume the entire responsibility for the promotion, operation and management of ARMX and to continue to so operate ARMX in the foreseeable future.
In summary, the agreement purely and simply absolves the Department of National Defence from all responsibility for the operation of the exhibition. I do not make this statement in an apologetic way. It also states absolutely clearly that there is no liability for cost, manpower or material unless such is asked for in writing by Defence Publications Limited and negotiated with the Department.
The first privately managed ARMX was conducted right here in Ottawa in June, 1987, at Lansdowne Park. I am not entirely sure why it did not draw the attention of the city's ever vigilant council at that time, but it certainly met the organizer's aims. Judging by the participation of industry, it has also met the needs of the creators of technology.
In introducing the motion, the mover made reference to "instruments of death in this industry of death". The question which must be asked, to which I can relate from a Saskatchewan perspective, is: Who are some of these manufacturers of instruments of death in this industry of death? The participants from Saskatchewan at ARMX

May 19, 1989
Supply
include SBC Case Ltd., a producer of transportation cases and containers. Those are terrible devices. Another is SciTech, scientific analysis. Should we not be allowed to develop scientific analysis in this country?
There is SED Systems, computer high tech systems design, purely a destructive industry.
What about International Road Dynamics, producers of road signs? This is evil. How will we fight a war if we do not know which back lane to turn down?
The Saskatchewan Department of Trade and Investment assists in attracting defence contracts to Saskatchewan, including the attraction of high tech and other related industries. Instruments of death indeed.
I would not want anyone to think that the Department ceased to take any interest in ARMX once it turned it over to the private sector. The Department does not manage the operation of ARMX, but it does assist Baxter Publications in some limited ways. For example, it encourages military personnel to attend. It will maintain a booth, as the Minister referred to earlier, and I understand that the booth is provided free. Among other things, businessmen can find out how to bid for government contracts.
It also will assist in validating seminar subjects and by providing the keynote seminar address each day.
The Department of National Defence is more convinced now than it ever has been that there is a significant purpose to be served by ARMX in assisting the Canadian Forces to acquire the most appropriate, affordable technology required to enhance future training efficiency and increase the cost effectiveness of training. For a Department that has just contributed $2.74 billion to deficit reduction in the coming five years, anything that can increase cost effectiveness is nothing short of a Godsend. I think it is to the credit of the Department of National Defence that years before these cuts, it was already sponsoring ways, such as ARMX, of ensuring that each taxpayer's dollar was producing the most effective results possible.
How does ARMX contribute to cost effectiveness? It does so by offering to display modem military equipment and training technology devices; by providing Canadian
and international industries with an opportunity to discuss equipment and training requirements in an informal environment; and by fostering industry to industry relationships between Canadian and international sources of training devices and equipment, thus providing a forum for potential investment and co-operation with Canadian industry.
Most important, I want to stress that enhancing future training efficiency through trade shows like it, ARMX contributes to developing our defence industrial base. I need not tell you, Mr. Speaker, nor Members of the House, how vital the defence industrial base is to Canada and indeed all western democracies and the world as a whole. What would we do in the face of aggression without an industrial capacity responsive to operational military requirements?
This is no longer 1939 or 1940. In 1989, as the military put it, if war breaks out you go as you are. There is no time to create an industry. More specifically industrial preparedness provides us with an assured source of essential defence materiel, services and technical capability. It also provides a strategic source of essential defence materiel to meet our defence needs under peacetime, crisis and mobilization conditions.
I could go on and on, but I feel I must now conclude. If I may, I want to emphasize and reiterate, because it will never be said often enough, that without ARMX we would not have this very unique opportunity to have industry and government meet informally to discuss one of the most important priorities any country has. That is to say, to become aware of the newest technologies known to man in our quest to maintain not only Canadian sovereignty but peace and security.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for his presentation this afternoon. It was very thoughtful and informative.
I have been listening with great interest both to the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party. It is my opinion that neither Party has its act together and cannot decide whether or not they are in favour of this particular show. We heard from the Member for Papineau-St. Michel (Mr. Ouellet) and the Member for Kingston and the Islands (Mr. Milliken). One was opposed to it and

the other supported it if we showed him the list of exhibitors and invitees.
The New Democratic Party is using this motion to talk about its philosophy as far as defence is concerned, which is convoluted at the best of times.
My colleague, the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mrs. Collins), has provided me with a brochure on an air show in Abbotsford, British Columbia. This is a show demonstrating aeroplanes of all makes from around the world, along with associated equipment.
Does the Hon. Member think that this air show in Abbotsford would be in violation of the policy of the New Democratic Party as it was presented to the House today in connection with the ARMX show?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT INVOLVEMENT IN ARMX'89 ARMS BAZAAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the my colleague for the opportunity to speak again. This is a subject in which I have an interest, which I think can be described as a realistic interest.
As I sat in the House this afternoon I sensed a lot of "nimbism", I think, that is to say: "not in my backyard, I think. We are not really 100 per cent sure of what is going on but at the risk of making a mistake let us condemn ARMX for something that it may be". As a result of that we seem to have this debate taking place when we could have so many more productive things before us.
With direct reference to the air show at Abbotsford, I cannot help but think that if members of the NDP were to sanction the event they would be doing nothing short of developing hypocrisy in the opinion of the individual who would in fact express that point of view. An air show, while it is intended to show the defence mechanisms our country has available to us, at the same time shows equipment that is used for attack purposes. It is extremely hard to develop a piece of equipment that can offset the impulse of an aggressor without at the same time providing some degree of attack in the same breath. I do not know how anyone for a minute could sanction the public display and the costs associated with it for that matter of defence and military equipment that we have which on the one hand provides us with defence while, on the other, offers us with a form of offence.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to share the same type of confusion that Members opposite are expressing with respect to ARMX. My confusion comes from the responses we have been receiving from the Government. I must accept, as my Party has always accepted, that the Government cannot ignore its defence responsibilities. There is no question that we do have responsibilities to safeguard our borders and our population and to protect our interests world-wide.
Where we do have a problem is in the discussion that has developed over the course of the day on ideology. We have a problem because the Government has indicated through its Ministers over the course of the debate that it is encouraging, participating, contributing, and involving itself in all manner of fashion in the promotion of ARMX. We have seen contradictions as stated by Ministers and Members on the government side about, first, a list of invited guests, and then about the confidentiality of such a list. I dare say there has been contradiction with respect to the type of promotions the Government must engage in, in order to ensure the success of what the Minister of State for Privatization (Mr. McDermid) referred to as a business enterprise, a commercial venture that would be of benefit to Canada economically.
There is nothing wrong with any venture that will assist the Canadian economy. What we would propose, though, is that the same type of enthusiastic vigour be addressed to conflict resolution on ideological grounds which is precisely the cause for a great deal of conflicts world-wide.
I would like to propose a question to my hon. friend. Perhaps he can seek the assistance of the Minister of State for Privatization to respond to it. The entire premise of the Minister is that this particular bazaar or bizarre, or whatever it is going to be, is to promote the commerce and well-being of the Canadian economy. I thought it might be appropriate for us to know which Canadian companies would be receiving assistance. I jotted down a few notes by way of question. I will go slowly for the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, looking at the clock I will try to hurry along as quickly as I can.
Certainly, it would be silly for anyone, any good Canadian, any freedom loving Canadian, to make the assumption that peace can simply either on the one hand be obtained by sticking one's head in the sand or, on the other, by flogging millions, billions and trillions of dollars. There is a path, a logical progression that seems to be on its way at the present time. I do not think that we can be blinded by the fact and the reality that this currently exists.
I would like to make a statement with respect to a comment made by the Hon. Member for Trinity-Spadi-na which is false. He says that there is military equipment that has gone to Chile and therefore we have allowed the export of weapons to be used where a military population represses the civilian population. This is false. Permits have been approved for Chile, but they are related to military equipment such as bomb disposal suits or communications equipment. I say that so it will not be left on the record unchallenged.
There was a term used that we should all dream for a better world. Indeed, I am sure when we go to bed at night we wish to dream for a better world. However, dreaming will not get that for us. We need only ask the Silver Cross Mothers on Armistice Day the price that they have paid for peace. Ask those who have fought in the wars what price they have paid for peace. It did not consist of dreaming. One cannot gain peace by dreaming. One gains peace by logical intervention. We gain peace by some show of defence and perhaps some position of sovereignty as related to one's abilities to equip oneself in such a way that one cannot be taken for granted.

I wish to quote the words of someone who said: "Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired, signifies in a final sense a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, from those who are cold and not clothed". So said General Dwight Eisenhower, President of the United States. If one does not dream of peace then it will never be achieved.
I believe that peace will be achieved if we really work within the two great institutions that we have. We must believe in disarmament. To achieve disarmament we

must keep our unity in NATO. We must be an extremely activist country within NATO. If we are not, we will never achieve true disarmament. We must not get out of NATO. That is one of the comments that was made earlier. If we left NATO, if we tell it to go its own way and we in Canada have our own personal policy on disarmament, then it cannot function.
As a last comment, I think that what is important is to work toward global disarmament within the institution that we have at our disposal.
Second, we must make sure that we start thinking of how to restructure the economies of the western world watching, of course, the economies of the eastern countries. We must restructure what has been for so
